title: NASA Human Research Program
note: Program overview for crew health and space radiation research.

title: NASA Human Research Roadmap
note: Health risks and knowledge gaps for human spaceflight.

title: NASA DONKI space weather database
note: Solar energetic particle, flare and CME records. Fetched by tools/fetch_donki.py.

title: NASA OSDR RadLab
note: Space radiation visualisation for context only. No number in the app is taken from it.

title: NASA Open Science Data Repository
note: Published spaceflight biology and physiology datasets.

title: PhysioNet database index
note: Physiological signal database index. Listed for reference; it is not the source of the demo ranges.

title: NASA Technical Reports Server
note: Searchable NASA technical reports.

title: ISS TEPC dose analyzer (CDAWeb HAPI)
note: Measured by the Tissue-Equivalent Proportional Counter (TEPC) on the ISS, a single station instrument, so this is a station-average rate, not a per-module value. Time-weighted mean of DOSE_EQ60 over 12 two-day windows spread across 2017 (windows with no reading were skipped): 0.884 mSv/day. Used as the ISS gcr_msv_per_day. Dataset covers 2010-04-29 to 2018-04-11; run tools/fetch_tepc.py to recompute.

title: Fermi GBM solar flare list
note: Solar flares seen by the Fermi Gamma-ray Burst Monitor. It gives peak counts per second, not a GOES class, so event severity is an assumption: log10(peak counts) scaled so 1,000 counts/s = 0 and 100,000 or more = 1. Flares alone are not dose events in this app (dose_relevant = 0).

title: Modelling assumption
note: A design choice made for this demo (score weights, model settings, routine timers, crew-protocol steps), not a measured or published value.

title: NASA HRP: 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight
note: Official challenge resource. Background on the five hazards of human spaceflight.

title: NASA HRP: Risks of Human Spaceflight
note: Official challenge resource. Background on the health and performance risks of human spaceflight.

title: NASA HRP: Ongoing research in space
note: Official challenge resource. Background on current Human Research Program studies in space.

title: CSA: Monitoring radiation for astronaut health
note: Official challenge resource. Background on how radiation is monitored for astronaut health.

title: CSA: Why do we conduct science experiments in space?
note: Official challenge resource. Background on why science is done in space.

title: Inspiration4 crew blood chemistry (NASA OSDR OSD-575, CMP)
note: Comprehensive metabolic panel of the 4 Inspiration4 crew members at 7 time points (L-92 to R+194), file LSDS-8_Comprehensive_Metabolic_Panel_CMP. Used only as context text for blood glucose (pre-flight mean 75 mg/dL, R+1 mean 93 mg/dL; lab fasting range 65-99). Very small sample from a 3-day flight; the app thresholds are not taken from it.

title: NASA Human Research Roadmap: Risk of Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS)
note: NASA's page for the SANS risk. Used only to show that SANS is a tracked NASA crew-health risk; no numbers are taken from it.

title: Mader et al. 2011, Ophthalmology: Optic disc edema, globe flattening, choroidal folds, and hyperopic shifts observed in astronauts after long-duration space flight
note: Abstract (read via Europe PMC, PMID 21849212): 7 astronauts after about 6 months on the ISS, 6 with decreased near vision; postflight questionnaires of about 300 astronauts: about 29% (short flights) and 60% (long flights) had worse distant and near vision; some changes unresolved years after flight. The app's ranges are not taken from it.

title: Lee et al. 2020, npj Microgravity: Spaceflight associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS) and the neuro-ophthalmologic effects of microgravity: a review and an update
note: Open-access review (PMC7005826). Used: visual acuity and Amsler grid are available on the ISS; about 15% of astronauts had clinically significant optic disc edema after long flights; choroidal folds in over 20%; all affected astronauts were correctable to 20/20 but some had residual refractive changes for several years; decreased near vision (hyperopic shift) was the main symptom. The app's ranges are not taken from it.

title: Heart rate limits: American Heart Association and NEWS2
note: Normal resting heart rate 60-100 bpm (AHA, All About Heart Rate). Watch below 50 and alert below 40 or above 130 follow the Royal College of Physicians NEWS2 chart: 41-50 bpm scores 1 point, 40 or lower and 131 or higher score 3 points (https://www.rcp.ac.uk/media/alxev00t/news2-chart-1_the-news-scoring-system_0_0.pdf).

title: Blood pressure limits: AHA, MedlinePlus and NEWS2
note: AHA: stage 1 high blood pressure starts at 130/80; above 180/120 needs prompt care. MedlinePlus: 90/60 or lower is low blood pressure (https://medlineplus.gov/lowbloodpressure.html). NEWS2: systolic 90 or lower scores 3 points, 91-100 scores 2 (https://www.rcp.ac.uk/media/alxev00t/news2-chart-1_the-news-scoring-system_0_0.pdf). No published diastolic-only low alert was found, so the app has none.

title: Blood oxygen limits: MedlinePlus and NEWS2
note: MedlinePlus: normal saturation 95-100%; contact a provider at 92% or lower, emergency care at 88% or lower. NEWS2: an oxygen saturation of 91% or lower scores 3 points (https://www.rcp.ac.uk/media/alxev00t/news2-chart-1_the-news-scoring-system_0_0.pdf), so the alert is below 92.

title: Body temperature limits: MedlinePlus
note: Normal 36.1-37.2 C (MedlinePlus Body temperature norms). An adult probably has a fever above 37.2-37.5 C, and over 38 C most often means a fever (https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003090.htm). Hypothermia is below 35 C (https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000038.htm).

title: Blood glucose limits: CDC and American Diabetes Association
note: CDC: below 70 mg/dL is low, below 54 mg/dL is severe. Two hours after a glucose drink, 140 mg/dL or below is normal (https://www.cdc.gov/diabetes/diabetes-testing/index.html). ADA: check ketones when blood glucose is 250 mg/dL or more for 2 hours (https://diabetes.org/living-with-diabetes/managing-ketones).

title: Reaction time limits: Basner et al. 2020 and Basner & Dinges 2011
note: Psychomotor vigilance test: alert people typically average 200-300 ms (Basner et al. 2020). Responses of 500 ms or more are lapses and responses under 100 ms are false starts (Basner & Dinges 2011, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3079937). Tablet touch latency can add time, so compare with your own baseline.

title: Body mass limits: CDC BMI categories at NASA astronaut heights
note: CDC: healthy weight is BMI 18.5 to under 25, obesity 30 or more. NASA astronaut candidates had to be 62-75 inches (157-190 cm) tall (NASA Facts, https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/606877main_fs-2011-11-057-jsc-astro_trng.pdf). BMI 18.5 at 1.57 m = 46 kg and BMI 25 at 1.90 m = 90 kg give the normal band; BMI 30 at 1.90 m = 108 kg is the upper alert. WHO: BMI below 16 carries a markedly increased risk of ill health (https://apps.who.int/nutrition/landscape/help.aspx?helpid=420); BMI 16 at 1.57 m = 39 kg is the lower alert. Change from your own pre-flight mass matters more: NASA reports typical in-flight losses of 1-5% (https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20150000512/downloads/20150000512.pdf).

title: Energy needs: NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2 Rev B, V2 7003
note: NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2 Rev B, V2 7003, Table 11 (activity factor 1.25): men EER = 622 - 9.53 x age + 1.25 x (15.9 x kg + 539.6 x m); women EER = 354 - 6.91 x age + 1.25 x (9.36 x kg + 726 x m), rounded to the nearest 10 kcal using pre-flight mass. When sex, birth year, height or pre-flight mass is missing, the app falls back to 2300 kcal/day. No upper limit is set. Measured ISS intake was about 2300-2450 kcal/day (NASA nutrition evidence report, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20150000512/downloads/20150000512.pdf).

title: Fluid intake: NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2 Rev B, V2 6029
note: At least 2000 mL of drinking water per crew member per day (section 6.3.2.1). The US National Academies set no upper limit for water (https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/10925/chapter/6), so the app has none. NASA's renal stone report says stone risk rises when urine volume drops below 1.5 L/day (https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20170004709/downloads/20170004709.pdf).

title: Urine colour: USADA and Wardenaar et al. 2021
note: On the 8-colour chart, keep urine below shade four (USADA, https://www.usada.org/spirit-of-sport/hydration-101-need-know/), so watch above 3. Published cut-offs for dehydration range from 3 or below to 5 or below (Wardenaar et al. 2021), so alert above 5.

title: Grip strength: EWGSOP2 (Cruz-Jentoft et al. 2019)
note: EWGSOP2 low grip strength cut-offs: below 27 kg for men and below 16 kg for women. These are cut-offs by sex, not severity levels. The app applies each astronaut's sex-specific cut-off as the watch limit (falling back to 16 kg if sex is unknown) and has no alert limit.

title: Elo, Leppanen & Jahkola 2003: single-item measure of stress symptoms
note: One question on a 5-point scale from 'not at all' to 'very much'. The authors count the top two answers ('rather' or 'very much') as stress symptoms, so the app watches at 4 (High) and alerts at 5 (Very high). Validated for groups, not for individual diagnosis.

title: UK ONS: national measurement of loneliness (2018)
note: Direct question 'How often do you feel lonely?' with five answers. 'Often or always' is the level counted as lonely (https://analysisfunction.civilservice.gov.uk/policy-store/loneliness-indicators/), so the app alerts at 1 (Very isolated) and watches at 2. The watch level is a convention, not a validated cut-off.

title: NASA space motion sickness grading (Davis et al. 1988)
note: NASA JSC grades: mild (no operational impact), moderate (minimal impact) and severe (significant performance decrement, may last beyond 72 hours). The app treats Mild as normal and alerts at Severe or worse. NASA's grades are given by a flight surgeon; the self-rating here is our adaptation.

title: LeBlanc et al. 2000, regional BMD loss on Mir (NASA slide, Sibonga 2007)
note: Slide 'Regional BMD losses Mir', %/month (n=16-18, LeBlanc et al. 2000): lumbar spine 1.06, femoral neck 1.15, trochanter 1.56, pelvis 1.35.

title: Sibonga et al. 2007, skeletal recovery after long-duration flight (45 crew)
note: Calcaneus loss of 2.9% at landing after an average flight of 173 days. Dividing by 5.7 months gives about 0.5% per month (our calculation, not a published monthly rate).

title: NASA HRP Evidence Report: Risk of Bone Fracture (2017)
note: Table 4: loss per month before ARED, trochanter 1.56% and lumbar spine 1.06%; with ARED 0.5% and 0.32%, a 68-70% reduction. The app lets exercise remove at most 50% of the loss.

title: NASA-STD-3001 Vol 1 Rev C, section 4.7.2 (bone)
note: Hip and spine bone density should stay at or above 95% of pre-mission (watch at 5% loss); femoral neck at or above 90% (alert at 10% loss).

title: NASA: Astronaut exercise
note: ISS crew exercise about 2 hours a day (see also CSA, https://asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/astronauts/living-exercising.asp). The app gives full exercise credit at 120 min/day.

title: NASA ARED update 2009 (NTRS 20090007467)
note: Exercise is prescribed per week, so the app averages exercise over the last 7 days.

title: Cucinotta et al. 2013, PLoS ONE: how safe is safe enough?
note: Uses about 20 g/cm2 aluminium as the typical spacecraft shielding; the app applies the mission background dose rate at this thickness.

title: GCR shielding: Chancellor et al. 2018 and NASA/TP-2005-213164
note: Added shielding removes at most about 25% of the galactic cosmic ray dose, reached by about 20 g/cm2 (Chancellor et al. 2018; NASA/TP-2005-213164, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20050196720). The app's exponential factor is set to match that (exp(-20/70) = 0.75); above 20 g/cm2 it slightly overstates the benefit.

title: Wilson et al.: Biological response to SPE exposures (NASA)
note: An August 1972 class event gives a dose rate of about 50 mSv/h behind 5 g/cm2 aluminium (model). The October 1989 events lasted about three days, so an event with no end time is given 72 hours (NOAA SWPC: radiation storms last hours to days, https://www.spaceweather.gov/phenomena/solar-radiation-storm).

title: Zhang et al. 2020, Science Advances: first measurements of the radiation dose on the lunar surface
note: Chang'e-4 LND measured 1369 microSv/day dose equivalent on the lunar surface behind about 3.5 mm aluminium, used as 1.37 mSv/day for the surface base. The rover uses the same value (assumption: similar thin shielding).

title: George et al. 2024, Nature: space radiation measurements during Artemis I
note: Dose equivalent inside the Orion cabin was about 0.96-1.24 mSv/day; the app uses 1.1 mSv/day for lunar transit.

title: Zeitlin et al. 2013, Science: radiation during the Mars Science Laboratory cruise
note: RAD measured about 1.8 mSv/day dose equivalent inside the spacecraft during the cruise to Mars.

title: Heart rate advice: AHA and NHS
note: Very high or low heart rate with chest pain, shortness of breath, dizziness or fainting is an emergency (AHA; NHS SVT, https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/supraventricular-tachycardia-svt/). The rest and re-measure times and the crew medical officer and ground steps are prototype steps.

title: Blood pressure advice: AHA and NHS
note: AHA: rest at least 5 minutes, no caffeine or exercise within 30 minutes; above 180/120 with chest pain, vision change, weakness or confusion is an emergency. NHS low blood pressure: drink water and stand up slowly (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/low-blood-pressure-hypotension/); lie down with legs raised if faint (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/fainting/). Re-measure times and crew steps are prototype steps.

title: Blood oxygen advice: MedlinePlus
note: Contact a provider at 92% or lower and get emergency care at 88% or lower. Sitting upright, a warm finger and the re-measure times are prototype steps.

title: Temperature advice: NHS and MedlinePlus
note: Fever: rest and drink plenty of fluids (NHS); one layer of lightweight clothing (MedlinePlus Fever). Low temperature: wrap in a blanket and give a warm non-alcoholic drink; below 35 C is an emergency (NHS hypothermia, https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/hypothermia/). Re-measure times and crew steps are prototype steps.

title: Blood glucose advice: CDC and American Diabetes Association
note: Low: take 15 g of fast carbohydrate and recheck after 15 minutes (CDC). High: drink plenty of water, check ketones at 250 mg/dL or more for 2 hours; vomiting, confusion or heavy breathing need urgent care (ADA, https://diabetes.org/living-with-diabetes/managing-ketones). CDC sick-day advice: keep taking diabetes medicine as usual (https://www.cdc.gov/diabetes/living-with/managing-sick-days.html). Holding food and the crew steps are prototype steps.

title: Sleep advice: NIOSH and CDC
note: Short naps of 15-30 minutes increase alertness (NIOSH). Avoid caffeine in the afternoon or evening (CDC, https://www.cdc.gov/sleep/about/index.html).

title: Back pain advice: NHS
note: Stay active and try exercises and stretches for back pain. The crew handbook posture is a prototype step.

title: Fluid advice: NHS and MedlinePlus
note: Drinking fluids regularly reduces the risk of dehydration; dark yellow pee and dizziness are signs (NHS). Too much water can lower blood sodium: headache, confusion and nausea are signs (MedlinePlus hyponatremia, https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000394.htm). Kidney stone risk: NASA renal stone report (https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20170004709/downloads/20170004709.pdf). Crew steps are prototype steps.

title: Dizziness advice: NHS and MedlinePlus
note: Move your head carefully and slowly (NHS vertigo); avoid sudden movements or position changes (MedlinePlus, https://medlineplus.gov/ency/patientinstructions/000692.htm). Crew steps are prototype steps.

title: Grip strength test: Roberts et al. 2011, Age and Ageing
note: Grip strength is recorded as the best or mean of up to three attempts. The other steps are prototype steps.

title: NASA OSDR Environmental Data Application (ISS cabin CO2, temperature, humidity)
note: Recorded ISS cabin environment data by mission period, viewable and downloadable. The demo shows simulated cabin readings; connecting this dataset is the next step.

title: Law et al. 2014: CO2 levels and reported headaches on the ISS, J Occup Environ Med 56(5):477-83
note: ISS CO2 ranged from 1 to 9 mmHg; keeping the 7-day mean below 2.5 mmHg keeps the risk of headache below 1%. Used for the level of the simulated cabin CO2.
